title: 5.3 Discrete independence
text:
Recall the definition of independence.
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if
\[
\text{P}(A \mid B)=\text{P}(A)
\]

By the definition of the conditional probability,
\[
\text{P}(A \mid B)=\frac{\text{P}(A \cap B)}{\text{P}(B)}
\]
We have
\[
\text{P}(A \cap B) = \text{P}(A) \cdot \text{P}(B)
\]

title: 5.3 Discrete independence
text:
Similarly, two RVs \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if
\[
p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=p_X(x), \;\;\; \text{for all $x$ and $y$ with $p_Y(y)>0$.}
\]

Knowing \(Y=y\) does not change our believe on how likely \(X=x\) occurs.


By the definition of the conditional PMF,
\[
p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{p_{X, Y}(x, y)}{p_Y(y)}
\]


\(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if
\[
p_{X, Y}(x, y) = p_X(x) \cdot p_{Y}(y), \;\; \text{for all $x$ and $y$.}
\]

title: 5.7 Joint expectation
5.7 Joint expectation
text:
Properties
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent
\[
\text{E}[X \cdot Y]=\text{E}[X] \cdot \text{E}[Y]
\]

If two RVs are independent, the expected value of their product is the product of their own expected values.

title: 5.7 Joint expectation
text:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{E}[XY] &= \sum_x \sum_y xy p_{X, Y}(x, y) \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{by 2-D LOTUS}}\\
&= \sum_x \sum_y xy p_{X}(x) p_{Y}(y) \;\;\;\;\;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{by independence}}\\
&= \sum_x \big (xp_{X}(x) \sum_y y p_{Y}(y)\big) \;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{factor out $xp_{X}(x)$}} \\
&= \sum_y y p_{Y}(y) \cdot \sum_x xp_{X}(x) \;\;\;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{factor out $\sum_y y p_{Y}(y)$}} \\
&= \text{E}[X] \cdot \text{E}[Y] \;\;\;\;\;\;\;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{by definition of expected value}} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5.7 Joint expectation
text:
Linearity of expected values
For any two RVs \(X\) and \(Y\), we have
\[
\text{E}[X+Y]=\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[Y]
\]

Note this property does not require independence.


More generally, for any \(n\) RVs \(X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n\),
\[
\small{\text{E}[X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n]=\text{E}[X_1]+\text{E}[X_2] + \cdots + \text{E}[X_n]}
\]

\[

\\

title: 5.5 Conditional PDF
text:
Conditioning
In the discrete case, the conditional PMF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is defined by
\[
p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{p_{X, Y}(x, y)}{p_Y(y)},  \;\; \text{if } p_Y(y)>0.
\]

In the continuous case, the conditional PDF of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is defined by
\[
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{f_{X, Y}(x, y)}{f_Y(y)},  \;\; \text{if } f_Y(y)>0.
\]

title: 5.5 Conditional PDF
text:
\[
p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{p_{X, Y}(x, y)}{p_Y(y)}
\]

\(p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)\) has the same shape as \(p_{X, Y}(x, y)\) at \(Y=y\) except that it is divided by \(p_Y(y)\), which ensure the normalization property.

title: 5.5 Conditional PDF
text:
\[
f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)=\frac{f_{X, Y}(x, y)}{f_Y(y)}
\]

\(f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)\) has the same shape as \(f_{X, Y}(x, y)\) at \(Y=y\) except that it is divided by \(f_Y(y)\), which enforce the normalization property.

title: 5.5 Conditional PDF
text:
Proof \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)dx&=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}dx \\
\\
&=\frac{1}{f_Y(y)}  \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{X,Y}(x,y)dx \\
\\
&=\frac{1}{f_Y(y)} \; f_Y(y) \\
\\
&=1 \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5.5 Conditional PDF
text:
The multiplication rule
In the discrete case,
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_{X, Y}(x, y) &= p_X(x) \cdot p_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \\
&= p_Y(y) \cdot p_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y) \\
\end{aligned}
\]
We can use this formula to calculate the joint PMF.

In the continuous case,
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{X, Y}(x, y)&= f_Y(y) \cdot f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)  \\
&= f_X(x) \cdot f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x) \\
\end{aligned}
\]
We can use this formula to calculate the joint PDF.

title: 5.5 Conditional PDF
text:
How are the joint, marginal, and conditional PDFs related to each other?

To calculate the joint PDF,
\[
f_{X, Y}(x, y)= f_Y(y) \cdot f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)
\]


To calculate the marginal PDF
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_X(x)&=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{X, Y}(x, y)dy \\
&=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_Y(y) \cdot f_{X \mid Y}(x \mid y)dy \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5.8 Covariance
text:
The covariance between two RVs \(\color{red}{X}\) and \(\color{blue}{Y}\):
\[
\text{cov}(\color{red}{X}, \color{blue}{Y})\stackrel{\text{def}}{=}\text{E}\big[\big(\color{red}{X}-\text{E}[\color{red}{X}]\big)\cdot\big(\color{blue}{Y}-\text{E}[\color{blue}{Y}]\big)\big]
\]























If \(\text{cov}(X, Y)=0\), we say \(X\) and \(Y\) are uncorrelated.

title: 5.8 Covariance
text:
Properties
\[
\text{cov}(X, X)=\text{var}(X)
\]

Proof
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{cov}(X, X)&=\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])(X-\text{E}[X])\big] \\
\\
&=\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])^2\big] \\
\\
&=\text{var}(X) \;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{by the definition of variance}}\\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5.8 Covariance
text:
Commutative property
\[
\text{cov}(X, Y)=\text{cov}(Y, X)
\]

Proof
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{cov}(X, Y)&=\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])\big] \\
\\
&=\text{E}\big[(Y-\text{E}[Y])(X-\text{E}[X])\big] \\
\\
&=\text{cov}(Y, X) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5.8 Covariance
text:
A shortcut formula
\[
\text{cov}(X, Y)=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\text{E}[Y]
\]

Proof
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{cov}(X, Y)&=\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])\big] \\
&=\text{E}\big[XY-\text{E}[X]Y-\text{E}[Y]X+\text{E}[X]\text{E}[Y]\big] \\
&=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\text{E}[Y]-\text{E}[Y]\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[X]\text{E}[Y] \\
&=\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\text{E}[Y] \\
\end{aligned}
\]

text:
Properties
\[
\text{cov}(aX+b, Y)=a\cdot\text{cov}(X, Y),
\] \[
\text{for any constants $a$ and $b$.}
\]

Proof
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{cov}(aX+b, Y)&=\text{E}\big[(aX+b-\text{E}[aX+b])(Y-\text{E}[Y])\big] \\
&=\text{E}\big[(aX+b-a\text{E}[X]-b)(Y-\text{E}[Y])\big] \\
&=a\cdot\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])(Y-\text{E}[Y])\big] \\
&=a\cdot\text{cov}(X, Y) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 5.8 Covariance
text:
Distributive property
\[
\text{cov}(X+Y, Z)=\text{cov}(X, Z)+\text{cov}(Y, Z)
\]

\[
\small{
\begin{aligned}
&\;\text{cov}(X+Y, Z) \\
=&\;\text{E}\big[(X+Y-\text{E}[X+Y])(Z-\text{E}[Z])\big] \;\;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{by def. of cov}} \\
=&\;\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X]+Y-\text{E}[Y])(Z-\text{E}[Z])\big] \\
=&\;\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])(Z-\text{E}[Z])+(Y-\text{E}[Y])(Z-\text{E}[Z])\big] \\
=&\;\text{E}\big[(X-\text{E}[X])(Z-\text{E}[Z])\big]+\text{E}\big[(Y-\text{E}[Y])(Z-\text{E}[Z])\big] \\
=&\;\text{cov}(X, Z)+\text{cov}(Y, Z) \\
\end{aligned}
}
\]

title: 5.8 Covariance
text:
Distributive property (cont’d)
Similarly, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{cov}(X, Y+Z)=&\;\text{cov}(X, Y)+\text{cov}(X, Z) \\
\\
\text{cov}(X+Y, Z+W)=&\;\text{cov}(X, Z) + \\
&\; \text{cov}(Y, Z)+ \\
&\; \text{cov}(X, W)+ \\
&\; \text{cov}(Y, W) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

text:

\[
\text{var}(X+Y)=\text{var}(X)+\text{var}(Y)+2\text{cov}(X, Y)
\]

Proof

=&\;\text{cov}(X+Y, X+Y) \\
=&\;\text{cov}(X, X) + \text{cov}(Y, X) + \text{cov}(X, Y) + \text{cov}(Y, Y) \\
=&\;\text{var}(X)+\text{var}(Y)+2\text{cov}(X, Y)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 2.11 Independence
text:
Properties of independence
If \(A\) and \(B\) are independent, so are \(A\) and \(B^c\).

Intuitively, if knowing that \(B\) has occurred does not provide any new information on how likely \(A\) occurs,
\[
\text{P}(A \mid B)=\text{P}(A)
\]
then knowing that the complement of \(B\) has occurred should also provide no information on how likely \(A\) occurs.
\[
\text{P}(A \mid B^c)=\text{P}(A)
\]


Proof:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{P}(A \cap B^c) =& \text{P}(A) - P(A \cap B) \\
\\
=& \text{P}(A) - \text{P}(A) \cdot \text{P}(B) \\
\\
=& \text{P}(A) \cdot (1- \text{P}(B)) \\
\\
=&\text{P}(A) \cdot \text{P}(B^c)
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 2.11 Independence
text:
Independence of three events
Event \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are (mutually) independent if
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{P}(A \cap B) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(B) \\
\\
\text{P}(B \cap C) &= \text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(C) \\
\\
\text{P}(C \cap A) &= \text{P}(C)\cdot\text{P}(A) \\
\\
\text{P}(A \cap B \cap C) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(C) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 2.11 Independence
text:
Independence of four events
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{P}(A \cap B) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(B) \\
\text{P}(B \cap C) &= \text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(C) \\
\text{P}(C \cap D) &= \text{P}(C)\cdot\text{P}(D) \\
\text{P}(D \cap A) &= \text{P}(D)\cdot\text{P}(A) \\
\text{P}(A \cap B \cap C) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(C) \\
\text{P}(A \cap B \cap D) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(D) \\
\text{P}(A \cap C \cap D) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(C)\cdot\text{P}(D) \\
\text{P}(B \cap C \cap D) &= \text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(C)\cdot\text{P}(D) \\
\text{P}(A \cap B \cap C \cap D) &= \text{P}(A)\cdot\text{P}(B)\cdot\text{P}(C)\cdot\text{P}(D) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 2.11 Independence
text:
Independence of \(n\) events
Events \(A_1, A_2, \cdots, A_n\) are (mutually) independent if
\[
\text{P}\bigg(\bigcap_{i \in S} A_i\bigg)=\prod_{i \in S} \text{P}(A_i)
\]
for every subset \(S\) of \(\{1, 2, \cdots, n\}\).

title: 6.2 Law of large numbers
text:
Law of Large Numbers (LLN)
Assume \(X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n\) are i.i.d. random variables with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).
\[
\bar{X}_n \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i
\]

Loosely speaking, the LLN states that with high probability, the sample mean \((\bar{X}_n)\) of many i.i.d. random variables is very close to the true mean \((\mu)\).


Note \(\bar{X}_n\) is not a number, but a random variable.

title: 6.2 Law of large numbers
6.2 Law of large numbers
text:
\[
\text{P}\big(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \epsilon \big) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\epsilon^2}, \;\; \text{for all $\epsilon > 0$.}
\]
For any fixed \(\epsilon\), the right-hand side of the inequality approaches to zero as \(n\) increases.

8.6 Two-sample z-test
text:
We know that \(\bar{X}-\bar{Y}\) is also normally distributed, and
\[
\small{
    \bar{X}-\bar{Y} \sim \text{N}\big(\mu_X-\mu_Y, \frac{\sigma_X^2}{m}+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n}\big)
    }
\]


\[
\text{Standardization:}\;\;\;\frac{\bar{X}-\bar{Y}-(\mu_X-\mu_Y)}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_X^2}{m}+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n}}} \sim \text{N}(0, 1)
\]

title: 8.6 Two-sample z-test
text:
\[
\text{We want to test if }\mu_X=\mu_Y \text{ (i.e., } \mu_X-\mu_Y=0)
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
&H_0: \mu_X=\mu_Y \; \text{ (or, } \mu_X-\mu_Y=0 ) \\
(1)\; &H_a: \mu_X \neq \mu_Y \;\text{ (or, } \mu_X-\mu_Y\neq0)\;\;\;\;\color{gray}{\rightarrow\text{two-tailed}} \\
(2)\; &H_a: \mu_X < \mu_Y \;\text{ (or, } \mu_X-\mu_Y < 0) \;\;\;\;\color{gray}{\rightarrow\text{one-tailed}} \\
(3)\; &H_a: \mu_X > \mu_Y \;\text{ (or, } \mu_X-\mu_Y > 0) \;\;\;\;\color{gray}{\rightarrow\text{one-tailed}} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

Regardless of \(H_a\), our test statistic is
\[
\small{
    z=\frac{\bar{x}-\bar{y}-(\mu_X-\mu_Y)}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_X^2}{m}+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n}}}=\frac{\bar{x}-\bar{y}-0}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_X^2}{m}+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n}}}=\frac{\bar{x}-\bar{y}}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_X^2}{m}+\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{n}}}
    }
\]

title: 8.6 Two-sample z-test
8.6 Two-sample z-test
text:
Large sample tests

When both sample sizes are sufficiently large, the CLT tells us that \(\bar{X}-\bar{Y}\) is approximately normal.
In addition, we can use the sample variance to estimate the population variance (often unknown in practice).


\[
\small{
    \frac{\bar{X}-\bar{Y}-(\mu_X-\mu_Y)}{\sqrt{\frac{s_X^2}{m}+\frac{s_Y^2}{n}}} \text{ is approximately } \text{N}(0, 1)
    }
\]
We can use it as the test statistic.


It is usually appropriate if both \(m>40\) and \(n>40\).

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Point estimation

Given a distribution parameter of interest (e.g., the probability a biased coin lands on heads), a point estimation is to use data to compute a number that represents an educated guess for the true value of the parameter.
The estimation (e.g., \(\hat{p}=0.9\)) is a single number, hence the name “point” estimation.
In upcoming lectures we’ll discuss interval estimation (confidence intervals).

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
A natural thought: select the parameters under which the observed data is most likely to arise.
That is, select the parameters that maximize the probability (likelihood) of obtaining the data at hand.

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

With a vector of \(n\) observations \[
X=(X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n)
\]

\(X\) can be described by

a joint PMF \(p_X(x; \theta)\) (if \(X\) is discrete)
a joint PDF \(f_X(x; \theta)\) (if \(X\) is continuous)



whose form depends on an unknown parameter \(\theta\).

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
\[
\text{With $n$ observations:}\;\;x=(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n)
\]
The likelihood function:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Discrete case:}&\;\;\;\;\mathcal{L}(\theta \mid x)=p_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) \\
\text{Continuous case:}&\;\;\;\;\mathcal{L}(\theta \mid x)=f_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

Important distinction:

A likelihood function is not the probability that the unknown parameter is equal to \(\theta\), given the observations \(x\).
Instead, it is the probability that the observations \(x\) would arise, assuming the unknown parameter is equal to \(\theta\).

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimate
A maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) is a value of the parameter \(\theta\) that maximizes the likelihood function:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Discrete case:}&\;\;\;\;\hat{\theta}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{\color{blue}{arg max}}}\; p_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) \\
\\
\text{Continuous case:}&\;\;\;\;\hat{\theta}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{\color{blue}{arg max}}}\; f_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

In maximizing the likelihood, we are essentially asking:
What is the value of \(\theta\) under which the data we received are most likely to arise?

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Standard procedure of MLE
Step 1. Obtain the likelihood function.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Discrete case:}&\;\;\;\;\mathcal{L}(\theta \mid x)=p_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) \\
\text{Continuous case:}&\;\;\;\;\mathcal{L}(\theta \mid x)=f_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

The following uses the discrete case as an example.
Assuming the observations are independent, we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
p_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta) &= p_X(x_1; \theta)\cdot p_X(x_2; \theta) \cdots p_X(x_n; \theta) \\
&= \prod_{i=1}^n p_X(x_i; \theta) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Standard procedure of MLE
Step 2. It is often more convenient to convert the likelihood function to the log-likelihood function.
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ln \big(p_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n; \theta)\big) &= \ln \bigg(\prod_{i=1}^n p_X(x_i; \theta) \bigg) \\
\\
&= \sum_{i=1}^n \ln \big(p_X(x_i; \theta)\big) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Standard procedure of MLE
Step 3. Maximization

Get the derivative of log-likelihood function w.r.t. \(\theta\).
Set the derivative to zero, and solve for \(\theta\).
Confirm that the second derivative at this point is negative.

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
\[\text{Data:}\;\;[2, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 2, 0, 0, 1]\]
The likelihood function for obtaining the above data
\[
\begin{aligned}
    &p_X(x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_{10};\theta) \\
    =\;&\text{P}(X_1=2, X_2=0, X_3=0,\cdots, X_9=0, X_{10}=1;\theta) \\\
    =\;&\text{P}(X_1=2;\theta)\cdot\text{P}(X_2=0;\theta)\cdots \text{P}(X_{10}=1;\theta) \\
    =\;&\bigg(\frac{\theta}{3}\bigg)^5 \cdot \bigg(\frac{2\theta}{3}\bigg)^2 \cdot \bigg(1-\theta\bigg)^3 \\
\end{aligned}
\]
Note the exponents (5, 2, and 3) are from the counts of zeros, ones, and twos in the data.

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
The log-likelihood function
\[
\begin{aligned}
    &\ln \bigg(\bigg(\frac{\theta}{3}\bigg)^5 \bigg(\frac{2\theta}{3}\bigg)^2 \bigg(1-\theta\bigg)^3\bigg) \\
    \\
  = & 5\ln\bigg(\frac{\theta}{3}\bigg) + 2\ln\bigg(\frac{2\theta}{3}\bigg) + 3\ln(1-\theta) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Get the derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t. \(\theta\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{d}{d\theta}\bigg(5\ln\bigg(\frac{\theta}{3}\bigg) + 2\ln\bigg(\frac{2\theta}{3}\bigg) + 3\ln(1-\theta)\bigg) \\
\\
=\;&5\frac{3}{\theta}\frac{1}{3} + 2\frac{3}{2\theta}\frac{2}{3}+3\frac{1}{1-\theta}(-1) \\
\\
=\;&\frac{5}{\theta}+\frac{2}{\theta}-\frac{3}{1-\theta}
=\;\frac{7}{\theta}-\frac{3}{1-\theta} \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Set the derivative to zero. Solve for \(\theta\).
\[
\frac{7}{\theta}-\frac{3}{1-\theta} = 0
\]
\[
\hat{\theta}=0.7
\]

title: 7.1 Maximum likelihood estimate
text:
Lastly we check the second derivative of the log-likelihood function w.r.t. \(\theta\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{d\theta}\bigg(\frac{7}{\theta}-\frac{3}{1-\theta}\bigg) &= -\frac{7}{\theta^2}-(-1)\frac{3}{(1-\theta)^2}(-1) \\
\\
&=-\frac{7}{\theta^2}-\frac{3}{(1-\theta)^2} < 0
\end{aligned}
\]
The second derivative is negative. Thus, \(\hat{\theta}\) is the value that maximizes the log-likelihood function.
In conclusion, the MLE of the parameter \(\theta\) is 0.7.

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
text:
Point estimate

Based on 80 samples, the battery life is \(\hat{\theta}=11.4\) hours.
It provides no information on how precise the estimate is.
Oftentimes, we are interested in constructing a so-called confidence interval (CI).
Roughly speaking, it is an interval that contains the parameter with a specified high probability (e.g., 95%).

The battery life has a 95% confidence interval of between 10.2 and 12.7 hours.

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
text:
Constructing a confidence interval

First, we need to specify a desired high probability.

This high probability is called the confidence level.
Common choices include 95% and 99%.
\(\alpha\) (equals to 1 minus the high probability) is often used to indicate the confidence level.



\[95\% \; \rightarrow \alpha=0.05\]


\[99\% \; \rightarrow \alpha=0.01\]

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
text:
Constructing a confidence interval

Once we specified the confidence level, say 95%, we aim to have a confidence interval with a lower and upper bound estimators \(\hat{\Theta}_n^{-}\) and \(\hat{\Theta}_n^{+}\)
so that


\[\text{P}\bigg(\hat{\Theta}_n^{-} \leq \theta \leq \hat{\Theta}_n^{+}\bigg) = 95\%\]

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
text:
Procedures for constructing a CI
Suppose \(X_1, X_2, \cdots, X_n\) are i.i.d. normal, with unknown mean \(\theta\) and a known variance1 \(\sigma^2\).

\[
\hat{\Theta}_n=\frac{X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n}{n}
\]


\[
\hat{\Theta}_n \sim \text{N}\bigg(\theta, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\bigg)\;\;\rightarrow\;\;\frac{\hat{\Theta}_n-\theta}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \text{N}(0, 1)
\]

Note this is a simple, albeit unrealistic case, as typically if we don’t know the mean, we don’t know the variance either.

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
text:
Procedures for constructing a CI
Let’s construct a 95% CI, that is, \(\alpha=0.05\).






\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi(\color{red}{?})&=0.025 \\
\Phi(\color{red}{?})&=1-0.025=0.975 \\
\end{aligned}
\]


It is called a critical value of \(z\) corresponding to \(0.025\).
We can check the standard normal table (next slide).

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
text:
We want
\[
\text{P}\bigg(-1.96 < \frac{\hat{\Theta}_n-\theta}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.96\bigg) = 0.95
\]

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
7.2 Confidence interval
text:
Rearange the sides.
\[
\text{P}\bigg(\hat{\Theta}_n - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \theta < \hat{\Theta}_n + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\bigg) = 0.95
\]
This means that
\[
\bigg[\hat{\Theta}_n - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\;\; \hat{\Theta}_n + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\bigg]
\]
is a 95% confidence interval.

More compactly, it can be written as \(\hat{\Theta}_n \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: 7.2 Confidence interval
7.2 Confidence interval
text:
It is a random interval centered at point estimate \(\hat{\Theta}_n\).
The half-width of the CI is \(z_{\frac{\alpha}{2}} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\).
The width of the CI indicates how precise the estimate is.

\[
\hat{\Theta}_n \pm z_{\frac{\alpha}{2}} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}

We often have a desired precision (i.e., \(\pm 0.5\) hours) and a confidence level (e.g., 99%) for a confidence interval.

\[

The sample size needed for a desired half-width of \(d\) is

title: 8.2 p-value
text:
Roughly speaking, p-values tell us how surprising the observed data is, assuming there is no effect.
p-value is defined as the conditional probability of getting a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the observed data, given that the null hypothesis is true.


\[
p\text{-value} \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \text{P}(\text{data} \mid \text{$H_0$ is true})
\]

It is not the probability the null hypothesis is true.



\[
p\text{-value} \neq \text{P}(\text{$H_0$ is true} \mid \text{data})
\]

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
Markov inequality
If a RV \(X\) is non-negative with mean \(\mu\), then
\[
\text{P}(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\mu}{a}, \;\; \text{for all $a > 0$.}
\]

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
Proof (For the discrete case):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu&=\sum_x xp_x(x) \\
&=\sum_{0 \leq x < a} xp_x(x) + \sum_{x \geq a} xp_x(x) \\
&\geq 0 + \sum_{x \geq a} ap_x(x) \;\; \color{gray}{\leftarrow\text{Since $x$ is non-negative}} \\
&= a\sum_{x \geq a} p_x(x) \\
&= a\text{P}(X \geq a) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
Similarly, for the continuous case:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mu &= \int_0^{+\infty} xf_x(x)dx \\
&=\int_0^a xf_x(x)dx + \int_a^{+\infty} xf_x(x)dx \\
&\geq 0 + \int_a^{+\infty} af_x(x)dx  \\
&= a\int_a^{+\infty} f_x(x)dx \\
&= a\text{P}(X \geq a) \\
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
\[
\text{P}(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\mu}{a}, \;\; \text{for all $a > 0$.}
\]

An alternative form: letting \(a=k\mu\), where \(k > 0\), we have
\[
\text{P}(X \geq k\mu) \leq \frac{1}{k}, \;\; \text{for all $k > 0$.}
\]

The probability that a non-negative RV takes a value greater than \(k\) times of its mean is at most \(1/k\).
The inequality is only helpful when \(k > 1\).
E.g., the probability of someone earning more than 3 times of the mean salary cannot be greater than 1/3.

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
Chebyshev inequality
If \(X\) is a RV with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then
\[
\text{P}\big(|X - \mu| \geq c \big) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{c^2}, \;\;\;\;\;\; \text{for all $c > 0$.}
\]

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
Proof
Let \(Y=(X-\mu)^2\). We know \(Y\) is non-negative.
Apply the Markov inequality with \(a=c^2\), we have
\[
\text{P}\big((X-\mu)^2 \geq c^2\big) \leq \frac{\text{E}[(X-\mu)^2]}{c^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{c^2}
\]
Event \((X-\mu)^2 \geq c^2\) is identical to \(|X-\mu| \geq c\).
Thus, we have
\[
\text{P}\big(|X - \mu| \geq c\big) = \text{P}\big((X-\mu)^2 \geq c^2\big) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{c^2}
\]

title: 6.1 Chebyshev inequality
text:
\[
\text{P}(|X - \mu| \geq c) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{c^2}, \;\; \text{for all $c > 0$.}
\]
An alternative form: letting \(c=k\sigma\), where \(k > 0\). We have
\[
\text{P}\big(|X - \mu| \geq k\sigma \big) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{k^2}, \;\; \text{for all $k > 0$.}
\]

The probability that a RV is more than \(k\) standard deviations away from its mean is at most \(1/k^2\).
E.g., the probability of someone’s salary is more than \(3\sigma\) away from the mean cannot be greater than \(1/9\).

\[X \sim \text{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\]

\\

\\

\]

Then we have \[\text{var}(X)=\text{var}(\sigma Z+\mu)=\sigma^2\text{var}(Z)=\sigma^2 \cdot 1 = \sigma^2\]

The correlation coefficient (or simply, correlation) between two RVs \(X\) and \(Y\):
\[

\]

We can rewrite it as
\[
\rho(X, Y) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \text{cov}\bigg(\frac{X-\text{E}[X]}{\sqrt{\text{var}(X)}}, \frac{Y-\text{E}[Y]}{\sqrt{\text{var}(Y)}} \bigg)
\]


The correlation is the covariance after standardization.

\]
\(\rho\) is dimensionless.

For any constants \(a\) and \(b\)
\[

&=\frac{1}{p_Y(y)} \; p_Y(y) \\

\end{aligned}
